title: The cross product: turning and the motor force

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the moment arrow along the bolt shrink as the shaded parallelogram of r and F flattens, then vanish with the push along the handle and flip past it, when you swing the push round.
interactive.title: The spanner and the bolt
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A spanner sits on a bolt, drawn in 3-D. The arrow r runs from the middle of the bolt to where the push meets the handle. The arrow F is the push. Together they span a shaded parallelogram. Its area is |r||F| sin θ, where θ is the angle between r and F. That area is the moment's size. The moment arrow, r × F, stands along the bolt, square to both r and F. A curved arrow round the bolt shows your right hand's fingers curling from r toward F. Your thumb points the way the moment arrow does. Out of the nut undoes it. Into the nut does it up. A readout under the picture gives the size and the direction. Small arrows marked i, j and k show the axes. Later the picture holds a wire between a north and a south magnet pole. The current I runs along the wire. The field B runs from pole to pole. The force on the wire stands square to both.
interactive.ignores: The push stays in the plane the spanner turns in. A real push with a part along the bolt also tries to bend it. Friction in the thread is left out. The moment is drawn whether or not the bolt moves. The field between the poles is drawn even. The wire is straight and the current steady. A real motor has many wires on a coil. Their forces turn it together. The general rule for working out any cross product from its parts comes later, with Matrices. The puzzles use example values, rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
The cross product of two vectors is a new vector. Its size is |a||b| sin θ. It points square to both. A spanner's moment and the force on a motor's wire both come from it.

You already work out a moment as the push times its distance from the bolt. That works with the push square to the handle. Now push at a slant. Call the arrow from the bolt to your hand r. Call your push F. Let θ be the angle between them. Split F into two parts. The part along the handle runs on a line straight through the bolt. It has no distance from the bolt to turn about, so it turns nothing. Only the part square to the handle turns the bolt. That part is |F| sin θ, the side opposite the angle. So the moment's size is |r||F| sin θ.[^1] This is also the area of the parallelogram that r and F span. Its base is |r| and its height is |F| sin θ. A 150 N push, 0.3 m out and square on, gives 0.3 × 150 = 45 N m. At 30° to the handle it gives 45 × 0.5 = 22.5 N m. Cos would give 45 × cos 30° = 38.97 N m. That number uses the part along the handle. That part turns nothing. With the push along the handle, θ is 0° or 180°. Then the moment is 0. Here is why three forces in balance must pass through one point, unless they are parallel. If their lines miss that point, they leave a moment. Then the body turns, so they cannot balance.

The moment also has a direction. r and F lie in the plane the spanner turns in. An arrow square to both must stand along the bolt. The [[right-hand rule]] says which way. Point your fingers along r and curl them toward F. Your thumb then points along the [[cross product]], r × F.[^2] To undo a standard right-hand thread, you turn it anticlockwise, seen from your side. Curl your right fingers anticlockwise and your thumb points at you. So the arrow points out of the nut to undo it. It points in to do it up. Swap the order and the arrow flips, so F × r = −(r × F). The axes follow the same rule: i × j = k, j × k = i and k × i = j. Turn any pair round and you get a minus, so j × i = −k. An arrow crossed with itself gives 0, since sin 0° = 0. The dot product is a plain number, but the cross product is an arrow. So 45 N m on its own is only half the answer. It does not say whether the nut comes undone or tightens.

The force on a motor's wire is a cross product too. A wire of length l carries a current I across a magnetic field B. The force on it has size IlB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the wire and the field.[^3] It acts square to both the current and the field. Point your fingers along the current and curl them toward the field. Your thumb gives the force. Say 10 A flows in 0.2 m of wire, square across 0.8 T. The wire feels 10 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 1.6 N. Line the wire up with the field and sin θ is 0. Then there is no force.

**The cross product is an arrow square to both vectors. Its size is |a||b| sin θ, and the right-hand rule points it.**

analogy.text: Think of screwing a length of conduit into a coupler. The conduit has a standard right-hand thread. Turn it clockwise, seen from your end, and it drives away from you. Turn it the other way and it backs out toward you. The moment arrow points the way that thread would travel. Swap the way you turn and the arrow flips.
analogy.breaks: The thread only travels when it turns. The moment arrow is there even when a seized bolt does not move. Also, the thread's pitch sets how far it travels. The arrow's length is set by how hard and how far out you push.

practice.text:
- Draw r from the pivot to where the force acts. For a motor, draw l along the wire, the way the current flows.
- Find θ, the angle between the two arrows when both are drawn from one point.
- For the size, multiply the two sizes together, then by sin θ.
- For the direction, point your right hand's fingers along the first arrow. Curl them toward the second. Your thumb gives the answer.
- Check that the answer is square to both arrows. Then write it with its direction, such as 45k N m.

**Rule of thumb:** Square on gives the most. Lined up gives nothing. Swap the order and the arrow flips. For a motor, Fleming's left-hand rule gives the same direction as the right-hand curl from current to field.

**Worked example:** Say you push 200 N on a spanner, 0.45 m from the bolt, at 60° to the handle. Square on, the moment would be 0.45 × 200 = 90 N m. At 60° it is 90 × sin 60° = 77.94 N m. On a motor, say a wire carries 20 A, with 0.3 m of it square across a 0.6 T field. It feels 20 × 0.3 × 0.6 = 3.6 N.

**Common mistakes**
- Giving only the size. A moment or a force needs its direction too.
- Using cos in place of sin. Cos gives the part along the handle, and that part turns nothing.
- Using the whole handle length when you push nearer the bolt. r runs to where the force acts.
- Swapping the order. F × r points the opposite way to r × F.
- Getting lost in an awkward view. Turn the drawing so the first arrow points right and the second leans up the page. Then the answer points out of the page, toward you.
